lessons.title: Stock car, not stock
lessons.objective: Explain why a stock car is not a showroom car.

payload.prompt: Which one is the race car?

image.alt: Two cars side by side: left is a street Camry with headlights and bumpers; right is a NASCAR stock car with no headlights, simplified body, and racing slicks.

options.text: The street car on the left
The stock car on the right

cues: Look for slick racing tires, no headlights, and a simplified body.

explanation.correct: Right. The stock car has purpose-built parts even though it looks like a showroom model.
explanation.incorrect: The stock car is the one with racing slicks, no street lights, and a reinforced cage. It is built to a strict rulebook, not sold in showrooms.

payload.prompt: Why are stock cars called 'stock' if they are not street cars?

options.text: They use old parts left over from past years.
Their bodies resemble showroom models but are purpose-built to a strict rulebook.
They are mass-produced on the same line as regular cars.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The name is a holdover from the days when racers really did race showroom cars. Today it only describes the look.
explanation.incorrect: Stock cars are called 'stock' because their outer shapes resemble showroom models, but every part inside is built to NASCAR spec and purpose-built for racing.

payload.prompt: Match the piece of the car to its role.

pairs.definition: The frame that holds the car together and carries the load.
Lightweight panels that give the car its showroom-like shape.
A steel structure that protects the driver if the car flips.
A custom-fitted seat that holds the driver in place during impacts.

distractorDefinitions: A painted layer that makes the car look faster.
A device that limits fuel consumption.

explanation.summary: Stock cars are built with a steel frame, lightweight panels, and layers of safety tech.

payload.prompt: What are stock cars built to?

explanation.correct: Right. Every car must meet the same spec for fairness.
explanation.incorrect: Stock cars follow a strict rulebook covering engine size, body shape and fuel tank capacity. The goal is cars that are close in speed, so teams and drivers decide the race.

payload.prompt: Are NASCAR chassis made of aluminum to save weight?

scene.alt: Overhead view of a chassis frame in the shop, tubes clearly visible.

choices.label: No, steel tube handles impact best.

explanation.correct: Right. The chassis is a steel-tube frame built to be stiff and to hold up in crashes.
explanation.incorrect: NASCAR chassis are steel-tube frames, not aluminum. Steel is stiff and tough enough for the loads and impacts of racing near 180 mph.

lessons.title: The Next Gen car
lessons.objective: Name what changed with the Next Gen car.

payload.prompt: When did the Next Gen car first race in Cup?

explanation.correct: Exactly. The Next Gen car premiered in 2022 and is still in use in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: The Next Gen car started in 2022. It replaced the old Gen 6 car and introduced symmetry, independent rear suspension, and single-lug wheels.

payload.prompt: Tap the independent rear suspension.

diagram.alt: Side profile of a Next Gen car showing symmetrical body, independent rear suspension arms, and single-lug center-lock wheel.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The independent rear suspension lets each rear wheel move independently.
explanation.incorrect: The independent rear suspension is a rear-suspension system where each wheel can move independently from the other.

payload.prompt: Match the Next Gen change to what it does.

pairs.definition: Left and right sides match, which cuts the number of parts teams need.
Each rear wheel moves on its own, improving handling over bumps.
One center-lock nut per wheel instead of five, but trickier pit stops.
Lightweight panels shared across all three brands for cost control.

distractorDefinitions: A new engine with more horsepower.
A special fuel blend for better mileage.

explanation.summary: Next Gen prioritized shared parts, cost control, and safety while keeping racing competitive.

statement.speaker: crew member
statement.text: The single-lug wheel cost us the race.

options.text: One center-lock nut made the pit stop slow or jam.
They ran out of fuel on the last lap.
The engine doesn't support single wheels.

payload.translation: The pit crew had trouble with the single-lug wheel nut.

followUps.line: Did the wheel stick on the hub during the stop?
followUps.why: It shows you know the single nut has to seat perfectly, and a jam costs seconds.

followUps.line: Was that harder than the old five lug nuts?
followUps.why: One nut sounds simpler, but it made tire changing a different skill from the old cars.

payload.prompt: Does the symmetrical body mean every car looks exactly the same?

scene.alt: Several Next Gen cars from different brands in a garage, each with its own paint scheme and sponsors.

choices.label: No, brands and paint still differ

explanation.correct: Right. Symmetry means the left and right sides match. Each brand still has its own nose and tail styling, and paint and sponsors make every car look different.
explanation.incorrect: Symmetry only means the left side mirrors the right. Brand styling, paint schemes and sponsor logos still make each car easy to tell apart.

lessons.title: Engines and horsepower
lessons.objective: Explain why horsepower differs by track.

payload.prompt: In 2026, how many horsepower do Cup cars make at superspeedways?

explanation.correct: Close. About 510 hp at Daytona and Talladega, held down by a smaller tapered spacer and a tall spoiler.
explanation.incorrect: Superspeedways (Daytona, Talladega, Atlanta) run about 510 hp in 2026, with a smaller spacer to keep pack speeds in check.

payload.prompt: What does the tapered spacer on top of the engine do?

options.text: Limits the air entering the engine, which reduces horsepower.
Improves aerodynamics by reducing drag.
Cools the engine faster on hot days.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A smaller spacer opening means less air and less power.
explanation.incorrect: The tapered spacer sits above the intake and restricts airflow. A smaller opening holds power near 510 hp at superspeedways; a larger one allows 750 hp at short tracks and road courses in 2026.

payload.prompt: What size is every Cup engine?
payload.template: All Cup engines are naturally aspirated {{size}} V8s.

explanation.correct: Right. 358 cubic inches is the size rule for all three manufacturers.
explanation.incorrect: Every Cup engine is a 358 cubic-inch, naturally aspirated V8, built by each manufacturer to the same rules. Power changes by track through the tapered spacer, not through engine size.

payload.prompt: Which engine is a V8?

image.alt: Two engine diagrams: left shows four cylinders in a line (inline-4); right shows eight cylinders in a V shape (V8).

options.text: The inline engine on the left
The V8 on the right

cues: Count the cylinders and look for the V shape.

explanation.correct: Right. A V8 has eight cylinders arranged in two banks of four.
explanation.incorrect: The V8 has eight cylinders in a V configuration. The inline engine on the left is simpler but lower power.

payload.prompt: Loose at Bristol with 750 hp. Where does the fix come from?

facts.label: Power package
facts.value: 750 hp, set by NASCAR for short tracks

options.label: Adjust balance at the stop
options.consequence: Tire pressure, track bar or wedge changes can tame the rear, and the power package stays as the rules set it.
considerations: Loose is a balance problem, not a power problem.
Pressure, track bar and wedge are the crew's tools.
The driver still has to manage the throttle.

options.label: Ask NASCAR for a smaller spacer
options.consequence: Power levels are set by NASCAR for each track type, so teams cannot choose their own.
considerations: The power package is a rule, not a setup choice.
Less power would not fix the balance anyway.

options.label: Tell the driver to be gentler on exit
options.consequence: It helps the rear hang on, but it only treats the symptom and costs lap time.
considerations: The real fix is still in the car's balance.

payload.expertNote: More power makes a car harder to drive, but fixing a loose car means changing the balance, not the engine.

lessons.title: Three brands
lessons.objective: Spot Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota nose cues.

payload.prompt: Which nose wears the Chevrolet bowtie?

image.alt: Three NASCAR noses, each with its brand badge: a gold bowtie on the left, a blue oval in the middle, three overlapping ovals on the right.

options.text: The nose on the left
The nose in the middle
The nose on the right

explanation.correct: Right. The bowtie is Chevrolet's badge. Ford's is the blue oval and Toyota's is three overlapping ovals.
explanation.incorrect: The badge is the quickest tell: the bowtie is Chevrolet, the blue oval is Ford and the three overlapping ovals are Toyota. The cars look alike at a glance because the rules keep them close.

payload.prompt: Match the brand to its badge and body.

pairs.definition: Wears the gold bowtie badge; races the Camaro body.
Wears the blue oval badge; races the Mustang body.
Wears the three-oval badge; races the Camry body.

distractorDefinitions: Paint color decides which brand a car is.
The brand is whoever owns the team.

explanation.summary: The badge tells you which manufacturer a team races for, which helps you follow brand rivalries and team alliances.

payload.prompt: Why does brand matter in NASCAR?

options.text: Each brand backs different teams and has loyal fans.
Different brands have different engine sizes.
One brand is always faster.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Fans are Ford, Chevy or Toyota loyalists, and sponsors tie to manufacturers.
explanation.incorrect: All three brands build 358 ci V8s to the same rules. Brand is about factory support, sponsors and fan identity, not a different kind of car.

options.text: She is loyal to Ford teams and drivers.
She works for Ford company.
Ford is faster than Chevy.

payload.translation: She follows Ford-badged NASCAR teams and drivers.

followUps.line: Who is your favorite Ford driver?
followUps.why: It is a warm question that invites her story and does not pretend you know the whole roster.

followUps.line: Have you always been a Ford person?
followUps.why: Brand loyalty is often a family story, so asking about it is a great way in.

payload.prompt: Is one manufacturer guaranteed to be faster?

scene.alt: Pit box with three cars: one Chevy, one Ford, one Toyota, all with similar looking pit crews and equipment.

explanation.correct: Right. All three brands follow the same rulebook and run the same tires and a common chassis. Speed comes from the team, not the brand. Who is ahead in a given year can change.
explanation.incorrect: Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota all follow identical rules. Speed differences come from team engineering, driver skill and setup, not brand.

lessons.title: Wings and lips
lessons.objective: Explain what a spoiler and splitter do.

payload.prompt: Tap the rear spoiler.

diagram.alt: Side view of a NASCAR car showing the rear spoiler blade and, at the front, the splitter lip under the nose.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The rear spoiler is the blade on the back that adds downforce and drag.
explanation.incorrect: The rear spoiler is the blade at the back. The front splitter is the lip under the nose that keeps air from flowing under the car.

payload.prompt: What does a taller rear spoiler do?

options.text: Adds downforce and drag, slowing the car but improving grip.
Reduces drag and makes the car faster.
Only affects the car's appearance, not performance.

explanation.correct: Right. Downforce improves handling but costs top-end speed due to drag.
explanation.incorrect: A taller spoiler increases downforce (keeps the car glued to the track) but also increases aerodynamic drag (slows it down). Teams balance these effects by track.

payload.prompt: Match the aero term to what it means.

pairs.definition: A blade on the rear deck that adds downforce and drag.
A flat blade under the nose that shapes the air going under the car.
Air pressing the car onto the track, giving the tires more grip.
Air resistance that holds the car back and costs top speed.

distractorDefinitions: The noise an engine makes at full throttle.

explanation.summary: Downforce buys grip and drag costs speed. The spoiler and splitter are the parts teams use to trade one against the other.
explanation.sayThisLine: More spoiler means more grip, but it drags you down the straights.

payload.prompt: What does the front splitter do to the air?
payload.template: The front splitter keeps air from flowing {{direction}} the car.

explanation.correct: Right. The splitter blocks air from going under the nose, creating a pressure zone that adds downforce.
explanation.incorrect: The splitter is a lip under the front bumper that prevents air from flowing underneath the car, which increases downforce and grip.

payload.prompt: In 2026, do Cup cars make the same horsepower everywhere?

scene.alt: A board listing power levels by track type: superspeedways, intermediates and short tracks.

choices.label: No, it changes by track type

explanation.correct: Exactly. In 2026 it is about 510 hp at superspeedways, 670 at intermediates and 750 at short tracks and road courses.
explanation.incorrect: Power is set by track type through the tapered spacer: less at superspeedways to keep packs from running away, more at short tracks and road courses. Those numbers are the 2026 rules and can change.

lessons.title: Tires and fuel
lessons.objective: Explain what Goodyear tires and E15 fuel mean for racing.

payload.prompt: Who supplies every Cup tire?
payload.template: All NASCAR Cup cars use {{brand}} slick racing tires.

explanation.correct: Right. Goodyear is NASCAR's sole tire supplier.
explanation.incorrect: Goodyear is the exclusive tire supplier to the Cup Series. Teams cannot choose another brand, so they all run Goodyear slicks.

payload.prompt: What is E15 fuel in NASCAR?

options.text: Fuel with 15% ethanol blended in.
A fuel that is 85% ethanol and 15% gasoline.
Fuel that burns at exactly 15% efficiency.

explanation.correct: Exactly. E15 is gasoline blended with 15% ethanol. NASCAR runs a race-grade version of it.
explanation.incorrect: E15 is 85% gasoline and 15% ethanol, the reverse of what option two says. Some street pumps sell E15 too, but the racing version is a higher-octane race fuel.

payload.prompt: Match the tire term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A racing tire with no tread, used on dry tracks for maximum grip.
A rubber mixture designed for high-speed friction and wear.
Speed lost as tires wear throughout a run.
Single nut per wheel on Next Gen cars (2022+).

distractorDefinitions: A tire for wet conditions with raised grooves.
A pit crew member who changes tires.

explanation.summary: Racing tires, falloff and changing methods define pit strategy and race dynamics.

payload.prompt: How many gallons does a NASCAR fuel cell hold?

explanation.correct: Close. The fuel cell holds about 20 gallons in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: A Cup car fuel cell holds approximately 20 gallons. Track length and fuel mileage determine pit strategy.

payload.prompt: Do racing slicks last the entire race?

scene.alt: Pit stop scene with crew members swapping black Goodyear slick tires.

choices.label: No, teams pit to change tires.
Yes, one set lasts all race.

explanation.correct: Right. Tires wear, lose grip and are changed during pit stops.
explanation.incorrect: How fast tires wear depends on the track, the compound and the car, but they always fade. Teams pit to change them, balancing fresh tires against track position.

lessons.title: Who does what
lessons.objective: Match crew chief, spotter, driver and pit crew to jobs.

payload.prompt: Match the team role to the job.

pairs.definition: Leads the team and calls setup changes and strategy from the pit box.
Watches from high above the track and talks the driver through traffic.
Steers the car and tells the crew how it feels so they can fix it.
Five people who service the car over the wall during a stop.

distractorDefinitions: The official who throws the flags at the start-finish line.

explanation.summary: The crew chief makes the calls, the spotter is the driver's eyes, the driver feels the car and the pit crew turns the calls into seconds gained or lost.
explanation.sayThisLine: The crew chief made the call and the pit crew executed it.

options.text: No car is alongside up high, so there is room to move up.
The high bank is clear of debris.
The engine is running at high RPM.

payload.translation: No car is alongside on the high side, so the driver has room to move up the track.

followUps.line: Does the spotter or the crew chief make the pit calls?
followUps.why: The crew chief calls strategy. The spotter handles traffic, so this shows you know who does what.

followUps.line: So the spotter is the driver's eyes?
followUps.why: Yes. They watch from high above the track and keep the driver safe in traffic, since the driver cannot see everything.

payload.prompt: What is the crew chief's main job?

options.text: Engineer and strategist on the pit box; decides pit calls and car adjustments.
Tells the driver how fast to drive.
Manages the pit crew's physical fitness.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The crew chief is the lead engineer and calls every pit stop and adjustment decision.
explanation.incorrect: The crew chief is the strategic and engineering leader. They make pit strategy decisions, authorize adjustments and steer the race from the pit box.

payload.prompt: How many crew go over the wall on a stop?
payload.template: A pit crew has {{number}} members over the wall during a stop.

explanation.correct: Right. Five: two tire changers, the jack man, the fueler and the tire carrier.
explanation.incorrect: Five crew members go over the wall: the two tire changers, the jack man, the fueler and the tire carrier. A sixth is a penalty.

payload.prompt: Caution, front left tire blistering. Pit or stay out?

situation.narrative: You run third under caution. The driver says the front left is overheating and the surface is lifting.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: About 30 laps left in the tank

options.label: Pit for four tires and fuel
options.consequence: You fix the damaged tire, add the fuel you need and keep speed for the last 40 laps, at a small cost in track position.
considerations: A caution stop is far cheaper than a green-flag stop.
You need fuel anyway to reach the end.

options.label: Pit for fuel and two tires
options.consequence: A faster stop gains track position, but you only change two of four worn tires, so the car may fade.
considerations: Which two tires matter: the blistered one must change.
It works if track position is worth more than speed.

options.label: Stay out and hope it holds
options.consequence: The tire keeps wearing and can fail, and with 30 laps of fuel you would have to stop under green anyway.
considerations: A failing tire is a safety risk.
A free caution stop is wasted.

payload.expertNote: A blistering tire is a warning sign. Teams use a caution to fix it, and the crew chief weighs tires against track position.

lessons.title: Safety and inspection
lessons.objective: Explain how safety tech and inspection shape the sport.

payload.prompt: What does the HANS device do?

options.text: Keeps the driver's head and neck stable during sudden impacts.
Monitors the engine temperature.
Adjusts brake pressure during a crash.

explanation.correct: Right. The HANS (Head and Neck Support) keeps the head from whipping forward in a hard impact, which cuts the load on the neck and skull.
explanation.incorrect: The HANS device sits on the driver's shoulders and is tethered to the helmet. It holds the head back in an impact so the neck and skull take less force.

payload.prompt: Why does NASCAR inspect cars after a race?

options.text: To confirm they still met the rules, so nobody gains a hidden edge.
To wash and polish them for the next event.
To decide next week's starting order.

explanation.correct: Right. Cars are measured against the rulebook, for things like height and weight, so no team wins with a part or setup the others cannot use.
explanation.incorrect: Inspection is about fairness: checking that a car stayed within the rules, such as height and weight. It has nothing to do with cleaning or the next grid.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fast is fine, as long as it is legal.

payload.prompt: Match the safety feature to its job.

pairs.definition: Steel framework that protects the driver if the car flips or is crushed.
Foam-filled wall outside the track that absorbs impact energy.
Shoulder collar tethered to the helmet that limits head and neck motion in impacts.
Mesh over the driver window opening that keeps arms and head inside the car.

distractorDefinitions: Padding on the pit box to prevent crew injuries.

explanation.summary: Safety is layered: a strong cage, energy-absorbing walls, head and neck restraints and a net all work together to protect drivers at speed.

payload.prompt: Is every car fully inspected after a race?

scene.alt: A car on an inspection platform being scanned and measured after a race.

choices.label: Yes, every car gets a full check
No, the winner and some others

explanation.correct: Right. The winner and a selection of other cars, some picked at random, get the detailed post-race check, so any car can be chosen.
explanation.incorrect: Not every car gets the full treatment. NASCAR checks the winner and some other cars, some chosen at random, so nobody can assume they will be skipped.

payload.prompt: Finish the inspection rule.
payload.template: NASCAR checks cars {{when}} to make sure they match the {{spec}}.

options: only at the start of the season

explanation.correct: Right. Cars are checked before and after races against one rulebook, so every team races under the same limits.
explanation.incorrect: Inspection is not a one-off or a favor to anyone. Cars are checked around every race against the same rulebook, and a failure can bring penalties.
